content: The text provided is a highly detailed and technical summary of various medical interventions and their effects, primarily focusing on pregnancy-related conditions and treatments. 1. Antibiotic prophylaxis for recurrent urinary tract infections (RUTI): Antibiotic prophylaxis was associated with 162 fewer cases per 1,000 women (ranging from 84 fewer to 197 fewer). The certainty of evidence was low due to severe unexplained heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect. 2. Antenatal anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis: The administration of anti-D immunoglobulin during pregnancy to prevent Rhesus alloimmunization showed a reduction of 3 cases per 1,000 women (ranging from 4 fewer to 5 more). The certainty of evidence was very low due to reliance on studies with small sample sizes, unexplained heterogeneity, and wide confidence intervals. 3. Preventive anthelmintic treatment during pregnancy: The use of anthelmintics for soil-transmitted helminths resulted in 2 more cases per 1,000 women (ranging from 8 fewer to 18 more). The certainty of evidence was moderate, with limitations including unexplained heterogeneity and wide confidence intervals. 4. Tetanus toxoid (TT) vaccination versus influenza vaccination: Tetanus toxoid vaccination was associated with 91 fewer cases per 1,000 women (ranging from 60 fewer to 110 fewer). The certainty of evidence was moderate, with limitations including small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals. 5. Interventions for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy: P6 acupressure versus placebo: P6 acupressure showed 58 higher cases per 1,000 women, with low certainty due to small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals. Auricular acupressure versus placebo: Auricular acupressure showed lower scores favoring the intervention group, but the evidence was of low certainty due to baseline imbalances and lack of blinding. Acustimulation therapy at P6 point versus placebo: This intervention resulted in 99 fewer cases per 1,000 women (ranging from 22 fewer to 121 fewer), with low certainty due to indirect outcomes and small sample sizes. Traditional acupuncture versus placebo: Traditional acupuncture showed low certainty evidence due to small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals. Ginger versus placebo: Ginger was associated with 464 fewer cases per 1,000 women (ranging from 16 fewer to 656 fewer), with moderate certainty. Ginger versus P6 acupressure: Ginger showed low certainty evidence due to small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals. Ginger versus chamomile: Ginger showed low certainty evidence due to small sample sizes and unexplained heterogeneity. Ginger versus metoclopramide: Ginger showed low certainty evidence due to small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals. Ondansetron versus pyridoxine-doxylamine: Ondansetron showed 208 more cases per 1,000 women (ranging from 65 fewer to 1,000 more), with low certainty. 6. Pharmacological treatment versus lifestyle changes: Evidence was of very low certainty due to small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals. Acupuncture versus no treatment: Acupuncture showed 450 more cases per 1,000 women (ranging from 35 more to 1,000 more), with low certainty. 7. Reflexology versus rest: Reflexology showed 809 more cases per 1,000 women (ranging from 41 more to 1,000 more), with low certainty.
